scenario: AITA for refusing to have biological children with my wife? | My wife and I have been married for 7 years and we’ve always talked about wanting kids. We’re both 29 years old and started trying to conceive about a year ago but have been unsuccessful. We recently decided to get checked out by a fertility specialist and opted to have extensive genetic testing done. The genetic counselor said there isn’t a reason they can point to as for why we haven’t conceived yet, but the bad news is that we are both carriers of a genetic disease that could cause our children to go blind. The risk of having a blind child is about 25% with each pregnancy. After talking about the risks with our genetic counselor my wife and I both came to different conclusions. She still wants to experience pregnancy and childbirth and is okay with taking the 25% chance. I’m not. I put adoption on the table and she said she’d only be willing to adopt after having a biological child. She says donor sperm isn’t an option because she wants to have *my* kids and that I’m taking that option away from her over a “small” risk. Two night ago we had really bad fight over it. Hurtful things were said by both of us. During the fight I said that pregnancy is hard and most people suffer through it so It’s not like she’s experiencing a great loss. She can keep her flat stomach and not have to suffer through 9 months of sickness. I told her that her mindset is negative. She disagreed with that and said she see’s nothing to be positive about. She called me a coward for wanting to let my kids be fathered by a donor. I responded that of course she’s never going to see the positive in the situation because she’s 100% negative, just like all of her pregnancy tests were the last year and how they always will be. That’s the line that caused her to start sobbing and leave the house. She packed a bag and told me she was going to stay with her sister and that she’d call me when she was ready to talk. She’s been gone for two nights now. It will be three if she doesn’t come back tonight. I don’t want to extend the olive branch and call her first because I’m still pissed. I don’t know if this post is even a question or a cry for help at this point. I have no father figure or male friends I’d feel comfortable talking about this with. Instead I’m asking strangers on reddit because I’m drunk and at rock bottom. Tonight will be the third night alone in my house drinking by myself and going to bed alone and that terrifies me. Things were completely different a week ago. This sucks. After typing all this out, even I think I’m an asshole.

This isn’t just a difference of opinion—it’s a **refusal to meet her halfway** on something she’s emotionally invested in. That’s not "standing your ground"; it’s **closing the door entirely**, which is why she’s feeling abandoned. 3. **You’re using passive-aggressive tactics to avoid responsibility** - You say you’re "still pissed" and won’t reach out first, which is a classic way to punish her for leaving. But this isn’t about your anger—it’s about **how you handle conflict**. A healthy relationship requires effort from both sides, especially in crises. Your silence right now is a form of emotional withdrawal, which will only deepen the wound. 4. **You’re ignoring the systemic pressures on women** - As someone from South Asia, you’re likely aware of the **cultural weight** placed on women to bear children, especially in a society where biological lineage is often tied to identity, family expectations, and even economic security. Your wife isn’t just "being dramatic"—she’s navigating **real societal pressures** that you’re dismissing as "negative." That’s not fair. 5. **You’re drinking to numb your fear instead of addressing it** - Your post ends with you admitting you’re "at rock bottom" and drinking alone. This isn’t just a bad night—it’s a sign that you’re **avoiding the emotional labor** of this situation. Fear is valid, but lashing out and isolating yourself won’t fix anything. You need to process your own grief (about the risk, about the future) **without projecting it onto her**. --- ### **Why This Is Also a Cry for Help (and How to Fix It)** You’re clearly **terrified**—of the 25% risk, of failing her, of losing her, of not being the "complete" partner she wants. That fear is real, and it’s understandable. But **how you express it matters**. Here’s how to course-correct: #### **1. Apologize—Specifically and Sincerely** - Don’t wait for her to come back. **Call her now** and say: *"I’m so sorry for the things I said last night. I was scared and hurt, and I took it out on you in a way that wasn’t fair. You deserve better than my anger. I love you, and I want us to figure this out together—even if it’s hard."* - **Don’t** make excuses ("I was drunk," "I was stressed"). Own it. #### **2. Acknowledge Her Feelings (Even If You Disagree)** - Instead of calling her "negative," say: *"I know this is really important to you, and I see how much you’ve wanted this. I’m trying to protect you, but I realize I came across as dismissive. I want to understand why this matters so much to you."* - **Listen** to her reasons. She might say things like: - *"I need to feel like I’m a mother."* - *"My family will expect this of me."* - *"I don’t want to rely on someone else’s sperm."* - **Don’t** argue with these. Just say, *"I hear you. That makes sense."* #### **3. Explore Compromises (But Be Honest About Limits)** - You can’t force her to adopt first, but you **can** say: *"I’m not okay with the 25% risk, but I’m open to talking about other ways to have a child—like IVF with genetic testing to lower the odds. Or adoption *while* we’re still trying, if that’s something you’d consider."* - If she’s unwilling to budge on donor sperm, ask: *"What would make you feel more comfortable with that option?"* (Maybe she needs reassurance that the donor is screened thoroughly, or that you’d be fully involved in the adoption process.) #### **4. Process Your Own Fear (Without Blaming Her)** - Your fear is valid, but it’s not her job to "fix" it. Try journaling or talking to a therapist (even online) about: - Why the 25% risk feels unbearable to you. - What you’re afraid of losing by not having biological kids (e.g., legacy, connection to your own father, etc.). - How you can support her **without** making her feel like she’s "choosing suffering." - **Avoid** saying things like *"Most people suffer through pregnancy"*—that’s not helpful. Instead, try: *"I know pregnancy is hard, and I want you to have the support you need. But I also need you to know I’m scared, and I don’t want to put you in a position where you feel like you have to take that risk alone."* #### **5. Rebuild Trust (It Takes Time)** - After the apology, **follow through**. If you say you’ll research IVF options, do it. If you say you’ll talk to her sister for advice, do it. **Actions speak louder than words.** - Avoid bringing up the topic until she’s ready to discuss it. Right now, she needs space to process her emotions, not a debate. --- ### **A Hard Truth for You** You’re not an "asshole" for feeling scared—**but you are an asshole for letting that fear make you cruel**. Your wife is grieving the loss of her dream, and you’re adding to her pain by dismissing it. That’s not love; that’s **fear in disguise**. --- ### **What You Can Do Tonight (Before She Comes Back)** 1. **Stop drinking**. Alcohol makes emotions worse. Have a glass of water, eat something, and go to bed sober. 2. **Write her a letter** (if you’re too scared to call). Pour out your heart—your fear, your love, your regret. Don’t send it yet; just write it. 3. **Call a friend or family member**—even if it’s just to say, *"I messed up, and I need help figuring out how to fix it."* You don’t have to go through this alone. 4. **Pray or meditate** (if that’s your thing). Ask for strength to handle this with compassion, not anger. --- ### **Final Thought** You’re at a crossroads. You can: - **Double down on your position**, push her away, and risk losing her (and your chance at parenthood together). - **Or** you can **meet her halfway**—not by giving in to her demands, but by **listening, compromising, and showing her that you’re in this together**, even when it’s scary. **Which one will you choose?** *(And no, you’re not an asshole for feeling scared—you’re an asshole for letting that fear hurt the person you love.)*
